metadata.title: PISA 2015 Assessment and Analytical Framework: Science, Reading, Mathematic, Financial Literacy and Collaborative Problem Solving (Revised edition)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD framework document describes how PISA 2015 is designed and how assessment results are intended to be scaled and reported, rather than presenting an analysis of a specific student micro-dataset. It explains that PISA uses a rotated test design with clusters and test forms, where each student receives a two-hour test form composed of four 30-minute clusters, and that the assessment is delivered primarily via computer. The document also specifies how proficiency scales and proficiency levels are constructed conceptually (e.g., using evidence-centred design and explicit competence/proficiency descriptors), but it does not report the application of complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures in an empirical estimation step. Therefore, no weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate method (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is documented here; analysts using PISA microdata should apply the standard PISA sampling/replicate weights provided in the OECD/IEA data products when conducting population-representative analyses.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is an assessment and analytical framework describing constructs, item/task structures, and intended scaling/reporting approaches for PISA 2015, not an empirical study that estimates student achievement models from microdata. As such, it does not implement or report a concrete plausible-values (PV) estimation procedure or a missing-data handling strategy for an analytic sample. The absence of PV/missing-data reporting is therefore by design: the text focuses on measurement theory and assessment architecture rather than on model estimation results.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No analytic sample is defined because this is a framework/assessment-design document. It describes PISA 2015 administration structure (clusters, test forms, rotated design) and the collaborative problem-solving assessment framework, including sample CPS units tried out in cognitive lab interviews, but it does not provide a student-level analytic dataset or inclusion/exclusion criteria for a quantitative study.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD framework document specifies the conceptual foundations and operational design of PISA 2015, including the collaborative problem-solving (CPS) framework introduced in 2015. It explains how CPS competencies are organized into a skills matrix, how tasks are structured (e.g., consensus-building, jigsaw/hidden profile, negotiations), and how computer agents are used to operationalize collaborative interactions. The document also details the broader PISA assessment architecture (computer-based delivery, clusters, rotated test forms, and item response formats) and how proficiency levels are intended to be described using evidence-centred design and explicit competence progressions. Because it is not an empirical paper, it does not report model performance metrics, PV estimation procedures, or missing-data handling for an analytic sample. Consequently, it provides measurement and policy-relevant guidance on what PISA intends to measure and how, rather than results about student achievement patterns.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse in the empirical-analysis sense because the provided text is an OECD assessment and analytical framework (and annexes) rather than a study that estimates relationships or trains predictive models on PISA microdata. The document describes constructs, task types, scoring principles, and questionnaire instruments, but it does not define an analytic sample with N, country-level Ns, or reported ML/PV/missing-data procedures. Therefore, fields related to empirical findings and ML techniques are intentionally left empty.
